title: Staying in step with contemporary rhythm: rock, swing and the twist
summary: Gil says he would want a Fender-bass dance band and explains why swing music lost its fire.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: wanted to just deal with one or two more quotations of yours here. As you say, I've always been in the rhythm of whatever the contemporary rhythm is. And I just have a feeling that that doesn't do you quite justice because the way it comes out it makes you sound as if you are a follower and I think you are more of a leader.
When I say the rhythm of it I mean, I mean if I go to a dance it would have to be a rock and roll dance.

Sure. I mean I can't dance anyway, but I mean if I went to a dance now, it would have to be with a band with a Fender (similar?) bass. You know a band with some kind of (stop sound). It wouldn't have to be like numbing like rock and roll that kind of hits you over the head with a hammer, three chords, I don't mean that, sophisticated, but I need, I think of that sound since it's there, it's there, right? And it turns you on right away. You dance, you move to it.

Whereas some, the reason it's here is because a lot of the swing band music was beginning to get bad. And they were playing that stuff and there was no real fire in it. It was all melody and harmony and

the tunes were beautiful and all that but there was no real thing going on. That's when the twist came in and broke it up a little bit because there was no eight beat in the music up until recently. It was always one two, one two, one two. It never had any kind of, you know, eight beat sound to it.
